title: Agni, the go-between
hookLine: the fire god once hid from his job, and the gods coaxed him back: why every puja still has a flame
carry: Agni carries the offering; the lamp invites her

cards: Even a god can want to quit. In one Rig Veda hymn, Agni, the fire, has had enough. His work is to carry the offerings to the gods, and he's afraid of it: the brothers who held that work before him are gone.
So he hides, in the waters and in the plants. The gods go looking, find him, and coax him back, promising him a share of the offerings. He agrees.
In the Vedic picture, fire has carried things between earth and heaven ever since. Which is why the Sri Sukta's first request isn't to the goddess at all. It's to the fire.

teach.h: JATAVEDAS: A NAME OF AGNI, THE FIRE.
teach.b: The verse ends, in paraphrase: O Jatavedas, bring Lakshmi to me. Jatavedas is a name of Agni. In the Rig Veda's very first hymn, Agni is praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who will bring the gods here.
Offerings go into the fire; the fire brings the gods. The word for bring is avaha: bring here, carry this way. Not go and get.
More like a host saying, please bring her by. Here's the teaching. In Hindu worship, fire is the go-between.
It's why a havan pours ghee and grain into a flame: the fire carries the offering. It's why a Hindu wedding is walked around a fire, with Agni as witness.

teach.h: A LAMP AT THE DOOR FOR LAKSHMI.
teach.b: It's why so many pujas end with aarti: a lamp waved before the deity, then families cup their hands over the flame and draw its warmth to their eyes and heads.
And it's why, at Diwali, small lamps line windowsills and doorsteps. In the Sri Sukta's picture, a light kept burning is how the goddess is asked to come.
The verse quietly assumes one more thing: you can't ask a fire for anything if none is burning. Someone has to keep it fed.
Some readers hear a plain lesson there: fortune is asked for through something you already keep alive at home. Today: string lights are pretty.
But a clay lamp with a wick in oil is an invitation, and lighting it is a prayer.

how: In Lakshmi worship and Vedic rites, the Sri Sukta is chanted before a lamp or sacred fire, and some households light small lamps at Diwali to welcome the goddess.

games.why: Agni is the go-between of Hindu worship: he carries the offering, and the lamp's warmth comes back as blessing.

practice: Picture a small household fire, low and steady: with each in-breath, lay one small stick on it; with each out-breath, watch it settle and glow, not too much, not too little.
If you pray, you can ask the fire, as the hymn does, to bring good fortune to your house, or speak to God in your own words; if you don't, let the flame stand for whatever you hope will come.
